Lessons.Title: Functions Involving Percent Change
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: translate repeated percentage growth or reduction into exponential function notation, identify factor and initial value, and verify that percentages apply to the current amount. Original first-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 5 Lesson 15, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/5/15/preparation.html and student activity https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/5/15/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source compares repeated percent change in several contexts; this is an original numerical example rather than a publisher task copy.

An entirely hypothetical $400 account with an assumed 10% growth at the end of each full year and no transactions follows A(t)=400(1.10)^t for whole years t≥0. Its values for years 0,1,2,3 are $400,$440,$484,$532.40. The percentage added in year2 is $44, not $40, since 10% now refers to $440. This is invented arithmetic rather than a financial forecast.

A hypothetical item priced $80, discounted by 25% twice consecutively, has final price 80(0.75)^2=$45 rather than $40. First discount leaves $60, second leaves $45; nominal percent discounts cannot be added without regard to the changing base. For a percentage drop r, factor 1−r; for rise factor1+r when r is expressed as a decimal.

Student task: match expressions, value tables and word contexts, explain the difference between the additive increase and compounding, and refute a statement that repeated 25% discounts equal a single 50% discount. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 each (max8): expression with domain, correct successive values, base-change explanation and a counterexample with proper units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Repeated percent increase
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each period multiplies the current amount by one plus the decimal rate.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A(t)=a(1+r)^t for the stated equal-length periods.

KeyConcepts.Title: Repeated percent reduction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each period retains one minus the fractional reduction.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compounding base
KeyConcepts.Definition: Percent change is computed from the current amount, not always the initial amount.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Recalculate the amount of change after every step.

WorkedExamples.Title: Model a second year's change
WorkedExamples.Question: Starting $400, increase 10% at the end of each year.
WorkedExamples.Method: Work from the explicitly fictional data and verify the original model, units and domain.
WorkedExamples.Check: First and second growth dollars differ, but multipliers both equal1.1.

WorkedExamples.Title: Repeat a discount
WorkedExamples.Question: An invented $80 item is marked down25% twice.
WorkedExamples.Method: Work from the explicitly fictional data and verify the original model, units and domain.
WorkedExamples.Check: Two 25% reductions leave56.25% of original price.

WorkedExamples.Title: Evaluate third year
WorkedExamples.Question: Find A(3) for A(t)=400(1.1)^t.
WorkedExamples.Method: Work from the explicitly fictional data and verify the original model, units and domain.
Steps: Multiply by1.1 for one further period.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding successive 25% discounts as a single 50% reduction
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The second discount applies to a lower base.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding a fixed $40 each year for 10% growth
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Subsequent percentage changes use the updated amount.

SummaryPoints: Repeated percentage change yields a multiplicative exponential model.
The growth factor for10% is1.1; the retention factor after25% reduction is0.75.
Successive discounts and increases operate on the new base.
Model validity and peer critiques require teacher review.
